newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN says deaths mount among refugees in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: UN says deaths mount among refugees in Zaire.

text.p: Officials of the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) on Wednesday reported an "alarming increase" in deaths among refugees, mainly from Rwanda, in isolated areas of eastern Zaire.

They told a news briefing there had been a sudden surge of mortality among children this week at emergency health centres in the village of Tingi-Tingi, south of the town of Lubutu, where 120,000 refugees have camped.

"The alarming increase in child mortality, if it is as seems certain a reflection of the situation among the overall population, is causing us very deep concern," UNICEF's deputy director for emergency programmes Peter McDermott said.

"And the deaths we know of are only the tip of the iceberg. We have no way of knowing how many people are dying outside our centres." Reports from other areas where refugees have gathered indicated their situation could be even more serious.

The refugees are Rwandan Hutus who fled deeper into Zaire rather than return home with the some 750,000 who decided to go back late last year after over two years in exile following the genocide against Tutsis in Rwanda in 1994.

On Tuesday, the UN refugee agency UNHCR said the refugees at Tingi-Tingi appeared to be under the control of Hutu extremists, who long sought to prevent a return to Rwanda, now ruled by a mainly Tutsi government.
The UNHCR said the death rate in the camp was between 11 and 15 people a day, mainly young men.
But UNICEF said its officials on the spot had recorded 23 deaths at the camp on Monday, 12 of whom were children under five, against three child deaths a day last week.

McDermott said lack of food after the long journey from the shores of Lake Kivu, where they had originally camped after fleeing Rwanda in 1994, had left the refugees -- who also include Zaireans -- weak and vulnerable to disease.
The main causes of death were diarrhoea and malaria.

McDermott and UNICEF spokeswoman Marie Heuze said the food shortage was exacerbated by the complicated logistics of delivering food to the area, 170 kms (106 miles) south-east of the major supply hub for the region at Kisangani.

UNICEF was flying one chartered aircraft with a capacity of only three tonnes three times a day between Kisangani and Lobutu with urgent supplies. The Rome-based World Food Programme was working to bring in more planes.

But McDermott said there was a growing problem of movement out of Kisangani where Zairean forces appeared to be preparing an offensive against rebels who hold a large swathe of eastern Zaire after driving out government troops late last year.
